reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / WHO Classification of Skin Tumours
clinicalPearls: A malignant tumour of sebaceous differentiation that most often arises in the periocular region from meibomian and Zeis glands, but also occurs at extraocular sites
Periocular lesions notoriously masquerade as a recurrent chalazion or chronic blepharoconjunctivitis, so a firm or recurrent eyelid lesion warrants biopsy
Pagetoid intraepithelial spread through the overlying epidermis or conjunctiva is characteristic and contributes to multifocal disease and margin difficulty
Histology shows lobules of atypical cells with foamy, vacuolated lipid-laden cytoplasm; lipid stains on fresh tissue and markers such as adipophilin and EMA support the diagnosis
Association with Muir-Torre syndrome links sebaceous neoplasms to mismatch-repair deficiency and internal (often colorectal and genitourinary) malignancy
Immunohistochemistry for mismatch-repair proteins can flag Muir-Torre syndrome and should prompt consideration of hereditary cancer screening
Treatment is complete surgical excision, often with Mohs micrographic surgery or wide excision with map (conjunctival) biopsies, and radiotherapy in selected cases
reference.pathophysiology: Sebaceous carcinoma is a malignant neoplasm showing sebaceous differentiation, thought to arise from the adnexal sebaceous glands, prominently the meibomian and Zeis glands of the eyelid. Tumour cells proliferate as lobules and sheets with atypical nuclei and characteristic finely vacuolated cytoplasm reflecting intracytoplasmic lipid. A distinctive feature is pagetoid spread, in which malignant cells migrate individually through the overlying epithelium of the skin or conjunctiva, producing clinically deceptive diffuse involvement and complicating margin assessment. A subset arises in the context of Muir-Torre syndrome, a phenotypic variant of hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, where germline mismatch-repair deficiency underlies both the sebaceous neoplasia and associated visceral cancers.
additionalDifferentials: Basal cell carcinoma of the eyelid
Squamous cell carcinoma and its in-situ forms
Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (for conjunctival pagetoid spread)
additionalInvestigations: Full-thickness or incisional biopsy of any suspicious or recurrent eyelid lesion
Lipid staining on fresh (frozen) tissue and immunohistochemistry including adipophilin and EMA
Map (multiple conjunctival) biopsies to delineate pagetoid intraepithelial spread
Mismatch-repair protein immunohistochemistry and consideration of Muir-Torre / hereditary cancer evaluation
Regional nodal assessment and imaging for staging in higher-risk tumours
Ophthalmic examination to assess conjunctival and orbital involvement
redFlags: Recurrent or atypical chalazion that fails to resolve or recurs after drainage
Unilateral chronic blepharoconjunctivitis unresponsive to conventional treatment
Loss of eyelash follicles (madarosis) or eyelid architecture over a firm lesion
Diffuse conjunctival injection with an underlying eyelid mass suggesting pagetoid spread
Personal or family history suggesting Muir-Torre syndrome and internal malignancy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on tumour size, extent of pagetoid spread, and stage; periocular tumours can recur locally and metastasise to regional nodes, and delayed diagnosis from chalazion masquerade worsens outcome. Complete excision of localised disease carries a reasonable prognosis, but advanced or metastatic disease is associated with significant mortality.
pitfalls: Treating a recurrent eyelid lesion repeatedly as a chalazion without biopsy
Underestimating margins because of occult pagetoid intraepithelial spread
Failing to test for mismatch-repair deficiency and missing an underlying Muir-Torre syndrome
Overlooking multifocal or extraocular disease in the staging assessment
management: Screen all patients with sebaceous carcinoma for Muir-Torre syndrome using a validated risk score, and refer to clinical genetics when risk is significant, especially with age under 60, multiple sebaceous neoplasms, or a personal or family Lynch-related cancer history

Complete surgical excision is the mainstay of treatment for localized disease, using wide local excision with clear margins or Mohs micrographic surgery with complete circumferential and deep margin assessment
Favor wider margins, in the 5 to 6 mm range where anatomy allows, since narrower 1 to 3 mm margins have been associated with recurrence in surgical series

Consider Mohs micrographic surgery over wide local excision for improved local control, particularly given the tumor's tendency for multicentric and pagetoid spread that can be hard to detect on standard sections
Reserve radiotherapy for selected or surgically difficult cases as an adjunct or alternative to excision, not as routine first-line therapy
Consider sentinel lymph node biopsy for eyelid tumors staged T2c or higher using the AJCC eyelid carcinoma staging system
Manage confirmed regional nodal disease with surgical lymph node dissection, individualized with specialist input

For distant metastatic or advanced disease, individualize management through a multidisciplinary tumor board and involve specialist oncology input, since no specific systemic regimen is established for this disease

Intensify local control and follow-up (Mohs, wider margins, closer surveillance) for periocular tumors, lower eyelid location, orbital extension, or larger lesions, given their association with worse prognosis
Provide structured long-term surveillance of the treated site and regional lymph nodes given substantial reported local recurrence risk and potential for regional or distant metastasis

Biopsy any suspicious or recurrent eyelid lesion that mimics chalazion or chronic blepharoconjunctivitis and fails to resolve, and refer confirmed or suspected cases to a multidisciplinary team including ophthalmic oncology and dermatologic or surgical oncology
Refer cases with orbital extension, nodal involvement, or suspected distant metastasis to a specialist multidisciplinary tumor board for staging workup and individualized treatment planning
